title: 1862 to 1910: Japonisme and the great exhibitions
body:
Victorian Britain did not discover Japan through Japanese companies. It bought Japan through a British diplomat's collection, a Regent Street shop, a handful of designers and importers, and a showman in Knightsbridge. Japan's government only took control of how it was sold in Britain at the very end of the period, with the 1910 exhibition at White City. That pattern, British intermediaries first and the Japanese state arriving later, is the same one lesson 1 found in today's restaurant market.

### The door opens: 1858 to 1862

Trade needed a treaty first. Lord Elgin signed the [Anglo-Japanese Treaty of Amity and Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Japanese_Treaty_of_Amity_and_Commerce) with the Tokugawa shogunate, the military government then ruling Japan, on 26 August 1858. Hakodate, Kanagawa and Nagasaki opened to British merchants on 1 July 1859. British traders could now buy Japanese goods at source.

The goods that came first were not chosen by Japan. They were chosen by British officials and merchants, for British taste.

### 1862: a diplomat's collection at South Kensington

The first large public showing of Japanese objects in Britain was at the London International Exhibition of 1862. Japan sent no official exhibits. The Japanese section was put together by Rutherford Alcock, Britain's first diplomatic representative in Japan, and by Captain F. Howard Vyse, the British consul at Kanagawa ([V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O130487)).

According to Japan's National Diet Library, it included lacquerware, swords, straw raincoats, lanterns and straw sandals ([NDL](https://ndl.go.jp/exposition/e/s1/1862-1.html)). An article on Oxford University Press's blog puts the section at more than 600 objects ([OUP](https://jvc.oup.com/?p=9661)). I did not find an official count to check this against.

A shogunate embassy of 38 people, led by Takeuchi Yasunori (竹内保徳), was in London and attended the opening on 1 May. Europeans praised the display. One member of the embassy, Fuchibe Tokuzō, wrote in his diary that it looked like old bric-a-brac and was shabby ([NDL](https://ndl.go.jp/exposition/e/s1/1862-1.html)). The embassy spent its time on the machinery halls, a dockyard and an arms factory.

That split is the first lesson of the period. The British were buying Japan as craft and exoticism. The Japanese visitors were shopping for industry.

### The shop: from Farmer & Rogers to Liberty

The route from exhibition to customer ran through Regent Street. In 1862 a 19-year-old, Arthur Lasenby Liberty, joined Farmer & Rogers, a shawl emporium there. The firm is believed to have bought much of the Japanese section after the exhibition and sold it through its Oriental Warehouse, which Liberty went on to manage ([OUP](https://jvc.oup.com/?p=9661)). Whistler, Rossetti, Albert Moore and William Morris are named as customers.

In 1875 Liberty set up on his own, with half a shop at 218a Regent Street, three staff and a £2,000 loan from his future father-in-law ([Wikipedia: Liberty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_(department_store))). He sold ornaments, fabric and decorative objects, especially from Japan and the East. His "art fabrics" borrowed from the kimono's loose drape.

Liberty and his wife travelled to Japan in 1889, fourteen years after he opened. His shop was selling a British idea of Japan to British customers, and the idea was good enough to build a business on.

### The designers and the importers

The craze needed a name and a look. The French critic Philippe Burty is credited with coining "Japonisme" in the early 1870s for the Western fashion for Japanese art and design ([Tate](https://www.tate.org.uk/art/art-terms/j/japonisme)). Tate names the painter James McNeill Whistler as the main channel of Japanese influence into British art, and the designer Christopher Dresser and the architect E. W. Godwin as the key figures in design. Their work became known as the Anglo-Japanese style ([OUP](https://jvc.oup.com/?p=9661)).

Dresser is the clearest case of a designer turning into a trader. In 1876 to 1877 he spent four months in Japan, representing the South Kensington Museum, and was asked by the Japanese government to write a report on trade with Europe ([Wikipedia: Dresser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Dresser)). Tiffany of New York commissioned him to buy a collection of Japanese goods while there. From 1879 to 1882 he and Charles Holme ran Dresser & Holme, wholesale importers of Oriental goods, from a warehouse at 7 Farringdon Road. Holme later travelled to Japan with the Libertys in 1889.

### Japan starts selling for itself

The Meiji (明治) government that followed the shogunate learned fast. Japan's first official appearance at a European exhibition was Paris in 1867 ([V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O130487)), and its first as the Meiji government was Vienna in 1873 ([NDL](https://ndl.go.jp/exposition/e/s1/1873-2.html)).

At Vienna an adviser, G. Wagener, argued that Japan should show finely made craft goods rather than machines that imitated Western ones. It worked. Thousands of fans sold out within a week, and a British trading company, Alexander Park, bought the Japanese garden buildings with their trees and stones. Afterwards the government set up Kiritsu Kōshō Kaisha (起立工商会社), a company to sell Japanese crafts abroad, which signed a contract with the same British firm. The aim was foreign currency.

This is the point where Japan first acted as a seller in Europe rather than a source of goods.

### 1885: Japan as entertainment

The mass market came through showbusiness. On 10 January 1885 the Japanese Native Village opened at Humphreys' Hall in Knightsbridge ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_Village,_Knightsbridge)). It was a private venture by Tannaker Buhicrosan. Around 100 Japanese craftspeople and performers lived and worked on site. Visitors paid a shilling, watched artisans at work, took tea served from lacquer trays and bought fans, toys and instruments in its shops ([Londonist](https://londonist.com/london/history/japanese-village-victorian-knightsbridge)).

About 250,000 people came in the first months. The Embassy of Japan says the first four months, Londonist says five ([Embassy of Japan](https://www.uk.emb-japan.go.jp/en/event/japanese_village.html)). Wikipedia reports over a million by February 1887. A fire on 2 May 1885 burned the hall down and killed a Japanese wood carver. It reopened that December and ran until June 1887.

The Japanese authorities did not cooperate. They worried it showed Japanese people as inferior to Westerners.

Gilbert and Sullivan's *The Mikado* opened at the Savoy Theatre on 14 March 1885 and ran for 672 performances ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mikado)). Gilbert had the idea before the village opened, but its residents coached his cast, and the first-night programme thanked them.

### 1910: the state takes the stage

The period closes with Japan presenting itself. The [Japan-British Exhibition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan%E2%80%93British_Exhibition) ran at White City from 14 May to 29 October 1910 and drew over 8 million visitors. About 2,271 Japanese exhibitors and almost 500 firms took part, and the Diet voted a large sum to pay for it.

The [Embassy of Japan](https://www.uk.emb-japan.go.jp/en/event/webmagazine/1910_exhibition.html) describes its purposes as celebrating the Anglo-Japanese Alliance of 1902, promoting trade, and presenting Japan as a modern nation and an imperial power. It included displays from Taiwan and Korea, and "villages" of Ainu and Taiwanese indigenous people. British newspapers mostly praised it. In Japan it was widely judged a failure, partly because of those sideshows.

### Who sold Japan to Britain, 1862 to 1910

| Seller | Example | What they sold | How it reached customers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| British officials | Alcock, 1862 | Their own collections | Public exhibition |
| British retailers | Farmer & Rogers, Liberty | Crafts, fabrics, decorative objects | Regent Street shops |
| British designer-importers | Dresser & Holme | Wholesale Japanese goods and a style | Warehouse to trade buyers |
| Showmen | Japanese Native Village | An experience, plus souvenirs | Ticketed attraction |
| Japanese state | Kiritsu Kōshō Kaisha, 1910 exhibition | Crafts, then a national image | Exhibitions and export agents |

### What this means if you look at it as a business

These points are my reading of the history above, not a sourced claim.

1. **Intermediaries capture the early value.** The people who made money from the first wave were the British who chose, framed and sold Japanese goods, not the makers. Lesson 1 found the same with Wagamama and YO! Sushi.
2. **Curation is the product.** Liberty sold a selection and a look more than any single object. Today's equivalent is the restaurant or shop that edits Japan for a British customer.
3. **Experience reaches the mass market first.** A shilling ticket to Knightsbridge reached far more people than Regent Street did. Events still do that job.
4. **Official Japan arrives late and with different goals.** In 1910 the state wanted prestige and alliance as much as sales. Expect the same mixed goals from Japan House and tourism bodies (lessons 13 and 16).

### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Japonisme | French term from the early 1870s for the Western craze for Japanese art and design |
| Anglo-Japanese style | British furniture and decorative design using Japanese forms, linked to Godwin and Dresser |
| Treaty port | A Japanese port opened to foreign merchants by treaty, such as Kanagawa or Nagasaki from 1859 |
| Tokugawa shogunate | The military government that ruled Japan before the Meiji era and signed the first treaties |
| Meiji (明治) | The era and government that followed the shogunate and used exhibitions to promote Japan |
| Kiritsu Kōshō Kaisha (起立工商会社) | Government-backed company set up after 1873 to sell Japanese crafts abroad |
| World's fair | A large international exhibition where countries showed goods to buyers and the public |

options: Japan's shogunate government, which sent official exhibits
British officials: Rutherford Alcock and the consul at Kanagawa
Arthur Liberty, buying for Farmer & Rogers
The Kiritsu Kōshō Kaisha export company
quiz.q: Who put together the Japanese section at the 1862 London International Exhibition?
quiz.why: Japan sent no official exhibits in 1862; the objects came from Alcock and Vyse. The shogunate's embassy attended, which makes the first option tempting, but it did not organise the display.

options: The Japanese visitors were mainly interested in selling crafts
The British had no real interest in Japanese objects
British buyers wanted Japan as craft and exoticism, while the Japanese visitors were looking at industry
The display was withdrawn after Japanese complaints
quiz.q: What does the contrast between European praise and Fuchibe Tokuzō's diary entry in 1862 show?
quiz.why: Europeans praised objects the embassy thought shabby, while the embassy studied machinery and dockyards. The first option reverses the point: selling crafts became Japan's strategy only later, at Vienna in 1873.

options: A Japanese-owned shop importing directly from Japanese makers
A government showroom for Japanese industry
A ticketed attraction with Japanese performers
A British retailer selling a curated, British idea of Japan to British customers
quiz.q: Which statement best describes Liberty's early business?
quiz.why: Liberty opened in 1875 selling Japanese and Eastern goods and Japanese-inspired fabrics, and he went to Japan only in 1889. It was not Japanese-owned, which is the tempting misreading given what it sold.

options: Japan's government set up a company to sell Japanese crafts abroad
Britain banned Japanese imports to protect its own makers
Japan stopped exhibiting crafts and showed only machinery
Liberty opened a branch in Tokyo
quiz.q: What changed after the 1873 Vienna exhibition?
quiz.why: Crafts sold well at Vienna, and the government created Kiritsu Kōshō Kaisha to earn foreign currency from them. The third option is tempting because the embassy had admired machinery in 1862, but the adviser at Vienna argued for showing crafts instead.

options: The 1910 exhibition was a private commercial venture; the village was state-run
The 1910 exhibition was organised by Japan's government for prestige, alliance and trade; the village was a private show the Japanese authorities did not support
Both were organised by the Japanese government
The village drew more visitors than the 1910 exhibition
quiz.q: How did the 1910 Japan-British Exhibition differ from the 1885 Japanese Native Village?
quiz.why: Buhicrosan's village was private and Japanese officials disapproved of it, while 1910 was a state project tied to the 1902 alliance. The first option swaps the two; and 1910's 8 million visitors far exceeded the village's roughly one million.
